children: New Pearson research reveals Australia's frontline talent is entering the workforce without the job-specific AI literacy they need.

SYDNEY, Nov. 24, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Childcare workers, electricians, nursing assistants, construction labourers, and bus and truck mechanics are among Australia's most AI-exposed roles by 2036, according to new research from
(FTSE: PSON.L), the world's lifelong learning company.
The Australian findings, part of Pearson's global

report series, challenge the prevailing assumption that hands-on, people-facing work is immune to AI disruption. Pearson's analysis found that AI's impact in Australia will not be confined to office workers, knowledge professionals or the technology sector, overturning one of the most persistent assumptions in the workforce debate.
The findings come as Jobs and Skills Australia's newly released
reveals that 13.6 million Australians now use AI tools in their daily lives, with adoption among 25-49 year-olds exceeding 70 per cent.
Taha Haidermota, Country Head, Pearson Australia, said:

"The conventional wisdom has become 'university degrees are at risk, learn a trade - they're safe from change.' But our data tells a more complex, nuanced story. By 2036, some of Australia's most familiar frontline occupations will look fundamentally different. The question is not whether AI will change these roles. Instead, it must be whether workers and the systems that support them are prepared.

"Australian workers shouldn't have to navigate AI disruption on their own. These people chose hands-on, service-focused careers, and the expectation that they'll independently build AI literacy on top of an already demanding job isn't realistic. The responsibility sits with educators, employers, industry bodies and government to make that training accessible, practical, and built into the work itself."
From childcare to construction: what the data reveals
Childcare workers are one of Australia's most exposed frontline service jobs:

Childcare workers represent the greatest combination of labour market demand and AI exposure across all blue-collar roles in Australia. AI will transform large administrative tasks within the profession, freeing workers to devote more time to direct child engagement, development support and safeguarding.
Tradespeople are not insulated from AI:

Electricians, construction labourers and bus and truck mechanics all rank among Australia's most AI-affected skilled trade roles. Construction workers will increasingly need to interpret AI-generated guidance and use digitally-enabled equipment; electricians will see AI accelerate predictive maintenance and diagnostics; mechanics will need to work confidently across conventional and alternative-fuel systems as vehicles become more software-driven.
Healthcare dominates the grey-collar list:

Nursing assistants, dental hygienists, radiology technicians, ambulance drivers and psychiatric aides all rank among Australia's most AI-augmented service and technical workers. The medical sector, representing some 1,458,000 workers, combines significant labour market demand with high AI augmentation potential.
Dental hygienists face the greatest projected AI exposure in healthcare:
They rank higher than nursing assistants, midwives and surgical assistants.
Women are on the frontline of AI disruption:

The most AI-augmented roles - childcare workers, registered nurses, midwives and dental hygienists - are overwhelmingly female-dominated according to ABS data. Without targeted upskilling investment, AI disruption could deepen existing inequity in sectors that are already undervalued and under-resourced.
Augmentation, not just automation: how frontline work is changing

Pearson's research is explicit that AI's impact on skilled trade, technical and service work is primarily one of augmentation - changing how work is done, not replacing the workers who do it. In childcare, healthcare and construction, the most human aspects of each role, including safeguarding, patient care, safety judgement, compliance, and relationship-building, are projected to remain irreducibly human. What changes is the volume of routine, administrative, diagnostic and logistical tasks that workers currently perform manually.
How skills must evolve

Australia's workforce readiness challenge is compounded by an existing skills shortage. According to Jobs and Skills Australia's 2026 Occupations Shortage report, 27 per cent of all analysed occupations suffer shortages, with nearly half of all technician and trades roles in shortage, including in construction, electrotechnology, health, and early childhood education. The list closely matches Pearson's AI-augmented findings, meaning many of the roles most in demand are simultaneously those facing the most significant task change.
Pearson's research identifies several practical priorities for employers, industry and government, including:
Embed AI literacy into existing training programs:

Upskilling doesn't require workers to start from scratch. AI tools relevant to childcare, construction, healthcare and transport can be introduced through existing VET frameworks and on-the-job training, reducing the burden on individual workers to self-educate.
Invest in role-specific, not generic, AI training:

A childcare worker navigating AI-assisted scheduling has different needs to an electrician using predictive maintenance tools. Training that is designed around actual task change in specific occupations will be more effective and more likely to be adopted.
Prioritise sectors facing the double pressure of shortage and disruption:

Childcare, electrotechnology, construction and health face simultaneous skills shortages and high AI exposure. Targeted investment in these sectors now will address both challenges together, rather than sequentially.

Methodology

Pearson's Australian findings are drawn from its global For Every Future report, published in September 2026 from captured data in August 2026. The Australian country spotlight analyses AI's impact on entry-level skilled trade, technical and service roles using Faethm, Pearson's proprietary workforce analytics platform, and O*NET, one of the world's most comprehensive labour databases. The research examines roles requiring no prior work experience or education beyond high school, assessing each role's AI exposure, encompassing both augmentation (AI changing how tasks are performed) and automation (AI replacing tasks entirely), combined with its economic relevance and labour market demand. The five most in demand roles in the Australian labour market were selected for detailed analysis.
